story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm excited to share a personal project that I've put a lot of love into.

This is Orrery[0], a Three.js-based visualization of our solar system. It allows the positions of the major bodies to be played and scrubbed through the years 1950 - 2050, with optional orbit path displays and various other visualization options.

The data comes from NAIF SPICE - a framework and set of open-source data kernels containing highly detailed space geometry data.

I was inspired to set out on this project when learning that NAIF SPICE, originally written in Fortran and C, lacks highly standardized JavaScript bindings. There are great Python (SpiceyPy) and Rust (Anise) bindings, among other languages, but nothing for JavaScript.

So, I developed tspice[1] to wrap the CSPICE library. It uses the Native API when running in Node, and an Emscripten binding around CSPICE when running in the browser. It uses a standardized backend abstraction that the runtime swaps in depending on which context its invoked with.

tspice offers an API that is meant to be a near-literal translation of the C APIs, along with higher-level functionality in separate namespaces. It also offers web conveniences like a dedicated web worker client (calculations can be intensive, you don't want them on your render thread) and caching.

tspice only wraps a subset of the CSPICE library, but it was enough that I wanted to build a simple visualization tool to test it. Eventually the visualization testbed became refined enough that it felt compelling on its own.

Although this is a hobby project, I'd love to hear suggestions and feedback on either Orrery or the underlying tspice library. If there are any folks in the planetary science community in particular who might be interested in tspice, please let me know if there are features that would make this more useful for you.

One feature I love is the ability to generate a share URL of a particular viewer state that you like. I'd really love to see any states that people find especially cool! One of my favorite views is this one[2].

Thanks for taking a look!

[0] Orrery repo: https://github.com/rybosome/orrery [1] tspice repo: https://github.com/rybosome/tspice [2] favorite orrery view: https://orrery.ryboso.me/dVPLbtswEPwX9qoIol4UdWtaB22RNEbsoii...

story_text.value: Evergreen Common Lisp implements tiered JIT compilation with on-stack replacement, and includes many other interesting features (fibers! JVM integration! static and dynamic linked binaries! tree-shaking! speculative optimization w/ deoptimization!) You can even run native Android apps on your phone and connect to them with sly (https://github.com/atgreen/evergreen-compose). It still has long way to go, and sometimes is comically bad, but the Android apps working is a milestone that is good enough to share v0.0.1. The Android apps build directly from asdf. You don't need any of the normal Android tooling, apart from adb (the debugger, to copy it to your phone and forward slynk ports). Made with AI, of course (>2k commits over 2 months).

story_text.value:
Like instagram, but all photos have a shelf life: they can be up for year, an hour or ten minutes, or up until they're viewed 100 times, 1000 times or a million times, etc.

The longer they're up, the more they fade - user chosen filters are applied gradually over the lifetime of the photo (be it measured in clicks or time), gradually obscuring it. At the end of its lifetime, the pictures faded / expired, and disappears, though comments remain.

This is a fun side project of mine, An experiment in digital persistence and scarcity. And, yes its vibe coded, built on replit.

Currently just a responsive web page (desktop, and works great on iOS devices, which I have). Native apps for android and iOS to follow should interest and time permit!

title.value: Show HN: Digital scarcity; app where photos gradually decay with time / views

story_text.value:
I built Soulor independently as a 16y/o high school student. It helps reading social situations with multiple perspectives, and helps users rehearse hard conversations by simulating others with analyses and suggestions, there are also companions that knows the full context if users choose to share that can chat with them naturally. It can be both serious and entertaining, by switching different world views, and it fully respects users' privacy by keeping all texts encrypted.

In order to achieve modest performance, I built multi-regional gateway and a fine-tuned model integrating both quality and responding speed. The models are served on GPUs via Modal, with a second adapter just for the simulation, and reply latency went from 7.9s to about 2.0s.

It already has several users and I'm building it up quickly. Happy to answer questions about the app or the tech, and any feedback is welcome.

story_text.value:
Pretty self-explanatory tbh. I kept hitting the same friction using LeetCode, the built-in editor has no real language support and none of the Vim muscle memory I rely on everywhere else. So I started building it in.

This is also where I love AI, I had started to work on it years ago, at first it was only snippets of most used classes (vector, string, etc...) and a few vim keymaps. Being able to tell Codex "Improve this, make no mistakes" is pretty fun.

Also side note, I've always used Leetcode as a game to practice problem solving (Graph Algorithms <3333), but I feel like now more than ever it is a good platform to code manually and challenge yourself, especially when vibe coding is so present. (I don't recommend grinding if you don't enjoy it tho)
